promotions.hypothesis: Each of the 101 refined A^T solves now carries one right-hand-side column instead of two (for D = 1), so SuperLU triangular-solve and residual-product work in the backward drops. The grid gradient execute phase should fall by roughly 10–25 ms below candidate 4's ~169–182 ms, with aLIGO proportionally less; other phases are unchanged. Outputs are no longer bitwise identical, for two reasons: r_cov comes from the forward's refinement, and the signal column's stop test no longer includes the covariance column. The differences should stay at refinement level (~1e-14 relative), so strict-vs-seed should pass with zero failing elements.

If the grid's signal cotangent passes the collinearity test, each backward row loses its last refined A^T solve (1 initial plus up to 3 correction triangular solves, plus residual products). The backward then has only the carrier adjoint solve left, so the grid gradient execute phase should fall well below candidate 6's ~110 ms, likely by 40–60 ms; aLIGO falls proportionally if it also triggers. If it does not trigger, the arrays will be bitwise identical to candidate 6 (grid 108746cc…, aLIGO e82569f4…) and timing unchanged. That case is expected, for example, when a detector phase makes the selection complex or the readout is differential. When it triggers, differences against the seed should stay at refinement level, with strict comparison passing at zero failing elements.

The parameter insertion, linking and detector-phase steps currently use generic indexing with traced index arrays. That emits dynamic index normalization, and `.at[].set` cannot assume unique destinations, so JAX's scatter JVP builds an id-tagging scatter/compare/select construction that the gradient program then has to transpose. Using builder-verified static unique indices with explicit gather/scatter should cut forward and gradient trace/lower and compile time by a few milliseconds on both setups. Outputs and gradients should stay bitwise identical, since these steps only copy and cast values. The size of the gain is unmeasured and could be within noise.

Candidate 2 (214b4fa, request dba4a2c9) is rejected. It passed the official benchmark on all 3 grid and 3 aLIGO runs, and its arrays stayed bitwise identical to the seed, including 14/14 generalization cases. But it made the large setup slower: forward 213–216 ms and gradient 203–209 ms, against candidate 1's ~179 and ~172 ms. Grid median 1.034 s. On aLIGO, forward and gradient were 1–2 ms faster than candidate 1 and the median was 0.621 s, but that does not offset the large-setup regression.

What this shows: batching rows (3-D gathers, `add.reduceat` along axis 1, stacking) costs more than the per-row Python overhead it removes. The backward does no factorization and two refined solves per row, yet still takes ~1.7 ms per row. So the SuperLU triangular solves themselves are the likely dominant cost, and that cost scales with the fill nnz(L+U).
